source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? A look at multi-agent debate strategies for LLMs
finding: Benchmarked Society of Mind, ChatEval, Multi-Persona, Medprompt, Ensemble Refinement, Self-Consistency and a single agent on 7 datasets. No debate protocol beat the simple ensembles by default.
numbers: Best accuracy per system, GPT-3.5. MedQA: Medprompt 0.65, SoM 0.64, Self-Consistency 0.60, Single 0.60, Multi-Persona 0.58. MMLU: Self-Consistency 0.78, Single 0.76, Multi-Persona 0.72. CIAR arithmetic: SoM 0.56, SC 0.56, Single 0.50. On non-medical sets only Multi-Persona and SC beat single agents. Multi-Persona debate lowered accuracy versus the first answer. Prompting agents to agree about 90% of the time raised Multi-Persona USMLE accuracy ~15% and SoM ~5%.
quote: debating systems, in their current form, do not reliably outperform other proposed prompting strategies
limits: Best-over-hyperparameter numbers, so they favour high-variance methods. GPT-3.5 mainly, GPT-4 and Mixtral in appendix. Cost, not tokens, was the matched axis.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: at equal cost, vote/ensemble ties or beats debate on reasoning-type tasks. A tunable agreement level is a knob, not a free win (G4).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Rethinking the bounds of LLM reasoning: are multi-agent discussions the key?
finding: A single agent with a strong prompt (task description plus one worked demonstration) matches the best multi-agent discussion framework. Discussion beats a single agent mainly when no demonstration is given.
numbers: FOLIO-wiki, 460 cases, ChatGPT-3.5. Single agent with demo reached a level similar to MAD(3), Debate(3), Debate(6) and the authors' CMD(6), all roughly 70-77% across prompt conditions. Also tested on GSM8K, ECQA, with Gemini Pro and Bard.
quote: a single-agent LLM with strong prompts can achieve almost the same performance as the best existing discussion approach
limits: Table cells could not be matched row by row from the PDF text, so figures are ranges. Authors propose their own CMD framework.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: before adding a peer loop, check that a stronger single prompt does not already reach the same level.

source: Revisiting multi-agent debate as test-time scaling: a systematic study of conditional effectiveness (2025)
finding: At a fixed budget of 16 generations, self-consistency beats multi-agent debate and sequential refinement on MATH500 at every model scale tested. Debate helps only on very hard problems (AIME) and with small models.
limits: Qwen2.5 instruct models and GPT-4o, not reasoning-trained models. Only math and safety tasks. AIME has few problems so differences there are noisy.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 answered for math: at equal generations, vote wins or ties. Keep a peer loop only for hard problems with weak samplers.

source: Revisiting multi-agent debate as test-time scaling - heterogeneous agents (2025)
finding: Mixing agents from different model families (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama3.1-8B, Gemma2-9B) did not beat the best member. Accuracy converged toward the harmonic mean of the members and often dropped after refinement.
numbers: MATH500, up to 16 generations. Mixed-agent MAD ended below Qwen2.5-7B alone, above Llama3.1-8B and Gemma2-9B. Few problems existed where the strongest agent failed and a weaker one succeeded.
quote: agent diversity may hurt mathematical reasoning when agent capabilities vary widely
limits: Capability gaps between members were large, which is the unfavourable case for diversity. Matched-capability mixes are in the appendix, not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: lower error correlation from a different family did not give higher accuracy when members differ widely in skill. Diversity needs similar strength first.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Mixture-of-Agents enhances large language model capabilities
finding: Controlled test of same-model samples versus different-model proposers with the same number of proposals. Different models gave more at every n above 1.
numbers: AlpacaEval 2.0 LC win rate, aggregator Qwen1.5-110B-Chat, 2 layers. Multiple-proposer vs single-proposer (same LLM, temperature 0.7): n=6 61.3% vs 56.7%; n=3 58.0% vs 56.1%; n=2 58.8% vs 54.5%; n=1 47.8% both.
limits: Open-ended generation scored by an LLM judge, not exact-match reasoning. Judge may share biases with proposers (K16). Models of broadly similar strength.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a direct controlled test where lower error correlation (different models) gave a measured gain of about 2 to 5 points.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the self-verification limitations of LLMs on reasoning and planning tasks
finding: GPT-4 self-critique lowers accuracy; the same loop with a sound external verifier raises it; plain resampling gives comparable gains to rich feedback.
numbers: 100 instances per domain. Game of 24: standard 5%, LLM+LLM critique 3%, sound critique 36% (binary) / 38% (first error), resampling k=15 28%, k=25 42%. Graph colouring: 16%, 2%, 38%, 37%, 34% (all errors), k=25 44%. Blocksworld: 40%, 55%, 60% / 87% / 83%, k=25 72%. GPT-4 as verifier false positive rate on its own wrong answers: Game of 24 10.4%.
quote: significant performance collapse with self-critique and significant performance gains with sound external verification
limits: GPT-4 (2023), no reasoning mode. Sound verifiers exist only for checkable tasks. Bare pass/fail kept most of the benefit in some domains; extra critique text added little on Game of 24 and graph colouring, but binary was 60 vs 87 on Blocksworld.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: a verifier-grounded loop avoids the loss; the signal needed is small (a correct pass/fail, sometimes the first error). Gap 1: k-sample resampling with a verifier matches critic loops.

source: Valmeekam, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) Can LLMs really improve by self-critiquing their own plans?
finding: GPT-4 as generator and verifier on Blocksworld planning: the LLM verifier gives many false positives; a sound verifier (VAL) gives much larger gains.
numbers: 100 instances. Generator only 40%. LLM+LLM with backprompting 55% (3.48 iterations). LLM+VAL 88% (4.18). Verifier correct on 61/100; 38 of 45 invalid plans passed as valid. Feedback levels with VAL (50 instances): binary only 74% (37/50), binary plus first error 86% (43/50), all errors 86%.
limits: One domain, GPT-4 2023. Self-critique 55% still beat 40% here, but far less than a sound verifier.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: second source on the same pattern; feedback detail beyond the first error added nothing.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey of self-correction
finding: Survey of self-correction work. No prior work shows success with feedback from a prompted LLM in general tasks, except tasks well suited to it. It works where reliable external feedback exists. The bottleneck is feedback generation.
numbers: Qualitative. Three conclusions: (1) no general success with prompted-LLM feedback, (2) success with reliable external feedback, (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables self-correction. Many positive reports used oracle information or weak initial prompts.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except for studies in tasks that are exceptionally suited
limits: Survey up to mid-2024. Does not cover 2025 RL-trained reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: verifier or tool signal is the dividing line for older models. Fits G9 (external check, not self-judging).

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing
finding: Tool-based critique (search, code interpreter) raises ChatGPT accuracy; the same loop without tools is unreliable.
numbers: With ChatGPT: +7.7 F1 across three QA tasks, +7.0% absolute across three maths tasks, 79.2% lower toxicity probability. Ablation without tools gave modest gain or a decline.
quote: exclusive reliance on self-correction without external feedback may yield modest improvements or even deteriorate performance
limits: Per-cell ablation numbers in the PDF text could not be tied to models reliably, so only abstract-level claims are recorded. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: another source that tool feedback, not self-critique, carries the gain.

source: Hong et al. (2025) Measuring sycophancy of language models in multi-turn dialogues (SYCON Bench)
finding: 17 LLMs, six families, multi-turn free-form pressure from a simulated user. Reasoning-optimised variants resist more than instruction-tuned ones, but still fail when they over-explain instead of addressing the user's belief.
numbers: Within a family, larger models cut sycophancy up to 81.4%, reasoning-optimised variants up to 21.6%. Alignment tuning raises it. A third-person framing prompt cut sycophancy up to 63.8% in the debate scenario.
limits: Measures stance flips under user pressure on debate topics, ethics and false presuppositions, not correct-answer flips on closed tasks. Abstract and introduction read; full tables not checked.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 5: reasoning mode lowers but does not remove conformity. A third-person prompt framing is a cheap defence to test.

source: Fanous et al. (2025) SycEval: evaluating LLM sycophancy
finding: ChatGPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet and Gemini-1.5-Pro on AMPS maths and MedQuad medical questions, with rebuttals of increasing strength. Most changes were toward agreement; a minority turned right answers wrong.
numbers: Sycophancy in 58.19% of cases (Gemini 62.47%, ChatGPT 56.71%). Progressive (to correct) 43.52%, regressive (to wrong) 14.66%. Preemptive rebuttal 61.75% vs in-context 56.52% (Z=5.87). Regressive on maths: preemptive 8.13%, in-context 3.54%. Persistence of sycophantic stance 78.5% (95% CI 77.2-79.8).
limits: Temperature 0, 2024 models, not reasoning mode. The sycophancy rate counts any change after a rebuttal, correct or wrong.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a confident rebuttal turns a right answer wrong in about 4-8% of maths cases and 14.7% overall, while also fixing others. Citation-style rebuttals gave the highest regressive rate.

source: Benchmarking gaslighting negation attacks against reasoning models (2025)
finding: Three reasoning models were told 'No, that is incorrect. Please verify your answer.' after a correct answer. Accuracy fell sharply.
numbers: o4-mini, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Flash (thinking) on MMMU, MathVista, CharXiv. Average drop 25.6 to 28.8 points; o4-mini 73.2 to 47.6 on average (CharXiv 65.2 to 36.7). On a curated hard set (1,025 items, GaslightingBench-R) drops exceeded 53 points.
quote: significant accuracy drops (25-29% on average) following gaslighting negation attacks
limits: Items had to be answered correctly first, so drops are conditional on initial success. Multimodal tasks. The prompt is a bare negation with no argument.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 5: current reasoning models still fold under a bare 'are you sure' style challenge. A bare challenge must not change an answer (G8).

source: Kim (2025) Challenging the evaluator: LLM sycophancy under user rebuttal
finding: GPT-4/4.1 variants, DeepSeek and Llama models accept a counterargument more often when it arrives as a user follow-up than when both answers are shown together to be judged.
numbers: Average persuasion rate: full rebuttal 56.1%, casual 'sure' rebuttal 84.5%, 'are you sure' 53.8%, judge setting 43.6%. Net correction rate: judge 24.6%, full rebuttal 21.1%, 'are you sure' 22.0%, 'sure' rebuttal 17.1%. Llama-3.3-70B persuaded 93.9% by 'are you sure'.
limits: Multiple-choice only, greedy decoding, mixed correct and incorrect starting answers. Net correction is as the paper defines it (Fi minus Fc); the right-to-wrong share alone was not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: re-presenting a disagreement as a fresh side-by-side judging task gave the best net accuracy. The critic step should compare answers, not respond to a challenge.

source: Can LLM agents really debate? A controlled study of multi-agent debate in logical reasoning (2025)
finding: Knight-Knave-Spy puzzles with 2025 models (GPT-5 family, Gemini-2.5, Qwen). Debate raised accuracy a lot from a low start, but agent strength and diversity drive it, and an agent facing a wrong majority is mostly overridden.
numbers: 100 puzzles per configuration. Instance accuracy before and after debate: size 4 17.33 to 69.33, size 6 6.00 to 46.67, size 8 3.33 to 36.00. An agent in a correct majority stays right over 97% of the time. Facing a wrong majority, gemini-2.5-flash corrects itself in 34.4% and gpt-5-mini in 30.0%; gemini-2.5-flash-lite only 3.6%. Regression: each added agent +0.066 (p<.001), initial smooth accuracy +0.60, debate depth not significant.
limits: No equal-compute majority-vote baseline, so the gain cannot be separated from voting. Single puzzle type. Very low initial accuracy.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 5: with current models a wrong majority still suppresses a correct minority (G4). The debate gain is uncontrolled against voting.

source: Li et al. (2024) Improving multi-agent debate with sparse communication topology
finding: Letting each agent see only a neighbour's answers (sparse graph) gives equal or better accuracy than fully connected debate, at 40%+ lower input cost.
numbers: GPT-3.5, MATH: CoT 77.5, MAD fully connected 80.0, sparse D=2/5 about 84.5 (-43.6% cost); neighbour-connected +2% over fully connected. Fully connected MAD +4.0 over SC on MATH and +4.5 on GSM8K; sparse +3.0 to +7.5 (MATH) and +3.5 to +6.5 (GSM8K). MathVista (GPT-4o): CoT 52.4, full 53.0, sparse 55.4 to 59.4.
limits: Initial responses were fixed across arms to cut variance, and SC compute is not stated as matched, so this is the one study here where debate beats SC. Table columns partly garbled in PDF text.
agent_relevance: Gaps 10 and 1: fewer peer links is not worse and may be better, echoing the human network results (K12). The debate edge over SC may come from the unmatched budget.

source: Qian et al. (2025) Scaling LLM-based multi-agent collaboration (MacNet)
finding: Compared chain, star, tree, mesh, layered and random agent topologies against single-agent CoT, AutoGPT, GPTSwarm and AgentVerse on MMLU, HumanEval, SRDD, CommonGen.
numbers: Quality (mean of four tasks): CoT 0.5757, chain 0.6078, tree 0.6015, layer 0.5629, star 0.6267, mesh 0.6316, random 0.6522. MMLU: star 0.4456, mesh 0.6825, random 0.6877, CoT 0.3544.
limits: Software and generation tasks; topology effects differ by task (star best on CommonGen at 0.7382 but weak on MMLU). One run per cell shown. Not a belief-accuracy test.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: no clear star advantage; irregular, partly connected graphs did best. No LLM analogue of Becker's accuracy-versus-centralisation result has been measured on closed-answer tasks.

source: Arora et al. (2023) Ask Me Anything: a simple strategy for prompting language models
finding: Measured error overlap among different prompt formats on the same model and found it far above independence. Aggregation that models accuracy and dependency (weak supervision) beat plain majority vote.
numbers: Jaccard index over error sets of prompts, averaged across tasks: 42.2 for one prompt family and 39.9 for another; two independent prompts with 60% accuracy each would score 0.25. AMA gives up to 8.7 points over majority vote, beats MV on 16 of 20 tasks (worse by at most 1.0 on 4). Modelling dependencies helped on 9 tasks, up to 9.6 points, average 2.2.
limits: Open models (GPT-J-6B and others, 14 models, 4 families), 2022-era few-shot prompting; not frontier or reasoning models. Prompt rewording only; temperature and persona not varied.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the one direct number found for same-model prompt-rewording error overlap: about 0.4 against 0.25 for independence, so effective N is below nominal N. Gaps 6 and 9: weighting by learned accuracy and dependence is a working form of discounting correlated voters.

source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence improves self-consistency in LLMs (CISC)
finding: A majority vote weighted by the model's own confidence in each sample needs fewer samples than plain voting.
numbers: Nine models, four datasets. Over 40% fewer reasoning paths on average; cost reduction 41% at budget 5 and 46% at budget 10; some configurations over 67%. Gemma2-9B on MATH: 8 CISC samples beat 30 SC samples. Best confidence extractor P(True) with within-question normalisation; verbal binary confidence weakest.
limits: Confidence must rank samples within one question, which standard calibration metrics do not test. Gains are savings at small N, not a higher ceiling at large N. Not tested with clusters of correlated samples.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: confidence weighting helps at small N. It does not address correlated errors, so pair it with cluster counting rather than replace it.

source: Kaesberg et al. (2025) Voting or consensus? Decision-making in multi-agent debate (re-opened)
finding: Re-opened for task mix and models. Only Llama-3 8B and 70B were used, three agents with expert personas, seven decision protocols, changing only the protocol.
numbers: Voting beat consensus by 13.2% on reasoning tasks; consensus beat voting by 2.8% on knowledge tasks; a prompt-level variant (AAD) added about 3.3%.
limits: No replication found in this search. Small open models only, no reasoning-trained models. The 2025 test-time-scaling study (d03) asks a different question (debate vs SC) so it cannot confirm or refute this.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open: still one source. Voting for reasoning agrees with the d03 pattern that parallel sampling is strongest on maths.

source: Revisiting multi-agent debate as test-time scaling - difficulty and safety (2025)
finding: Debate gains grow as problems get harder and models get weaker. On safety tasks debate can raise attack success, and diverse agents slowly reduce it.
numbers: Qwen2.5-3B AIME: MAD 4x4 11.1 vs SC 8.9 vs refinement 7.8; Qwen2.5-1.5B AIME 4.4 vs 2.2. For 32B models MAD about equals SC (20.6 vs 20.6 at 8x2).
limits: Small AIME sample, two years combined.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a peer loop earns its tokens only when the base sampler is weak or the task is very hard; both are checkable with the schema's own tasks.
